newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL UNLIKELY TO EXPORT ALL SOYBEANS REGISTERED.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL UNLIKELY TO EXPORT ALL SOYBEANS REGISTERED.

text.p: Brazil is unlikely to ship all the 8.7 million tonnes soybeans registered for export by July 31, but estimates of how much domestic industries will buy back vary wildly, traders said.

Export registrations were up sharply from 3.59 million tonnes at the same time last year, according to government figures released by the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries (Abiove) earlier this week.

But few traders believed the whole amount would actually be exported. "It's very difficult to justify shipping beans out when you're probably going to have to import them later," said David Brew, trader at Brasoja.
Internal demand has dried up, with 91 percent of the 1996/97 harvest already committed by end July, according to independent consultant Safras e Mercado.
But estimates of "wash-out" -- when companies who have sold the product for export on paper later buy it back -- ranged from 200,000 tonnes to 1.5 million tonnes, depending on the source.
"A lot of people are talking about (a total of) seven million tonnes (of exports) because the internal market is so much better than exporting," said Brew.
Producers were receiving 18.00 reais ($16.60) per 60-kg bag in Ponta Grossa and 16.30 reais in Cascavel, the Parana state agricultural secretariat said in a daily report Thursday.

Soymeal and soyoil prices have been steadily climbing as the market is expecting a sharp drop in processing activity in the second half of the year, with some firms seen closing in September due to lack of raw materials.
"There is going to be a very sharp slowdown in the second half," said Fabio Trigueirinho, secretary general of Abiove. "The number of units that will be operating will be much smaller than usual."

But some traders pointed out the amount of wash-out would be limited by a number of factors. Companies can only buy back product at a lower price than they sold it, potentially complicating the deal, said one soymeal trader.
"I think there will be a maximum of 200,000 tonnes wash-out from registrations," he said. "There is not the slightest chance exports will only be seven million tonnes."
In addition, there was not enough merchandise available in August for companies to easily buy back as in most cases vessels were already lined up to load the product, he said.
Some 5.7 million tonnes soybeans had actually been exported by end July according to the companies monitored by Abiove, indicating there would be some wash-out, Trigueirinho said.

But he was reluctant to give a specific number, pointing out that despite expectations Brazil would not export as much as 8.7 million tonnes soybeans, export registrations had risen steadily in June and July when they should have stabilized.
"In my opinion we'll export at least eight million," Trigueirinho said. Abiove has officially forecast soybean exports will reach 8.5 million tonnes in the 1997/98 marketing year (February/January).
Brazil was seen importing heavily from the United States from October onwards, with most traders estimating up to one million tonnes of new crop U.S. soybeans will be brought in.
However, only those industries located close to ports will be able to import profitably, unless domestic soymeal and soyoil prices rise considerably.
These firms include Ceval Alimentos, which has facilities at Sao Francisco do Sul, Santista and Bianchini at Rio Grande port and Sadia and cooperative Coamo at Paranagua.
